analysis.one_liner: Gives family members of deployed service members two weeks of job-protected leave a year.
analysis.headline: The Military Family Leave Act drew 40 cosponsors, including two Republicans, but never received a hearing or a vote in the House Veterans' Affairs Committee before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let a spouse, son, daughter, or parent of a service member called up or deployed to a combat-related operation take two workweeks of leave each year, intermittently if they choose. The leave can be paid or unpaid at the employer's discretion, and the employer can ask for proof like a copy of the deployment order. Workers on this leave are guaranteed their same job or an equivalent one back, and employers cannot interfere with or punish them for using it.
analysis.who_benefits: Military families whose loved one is called up or deployed: a spouse, child, or parent could take time off to help with the call-up and the deployment period without losing their job. Families could take the leave in short bursts rather than all at once, and would not have to burn their accrued vacation unless they chose to.

how_it_helps.text: Entitles an employed spouse, son, daughter, or parent of a called-up or deployed service member to two workweeks of leave per year per family member deployed [S2][S3].
Leave may be taken intermittently or on a reduced schedule, so a worker could take a day or a few hours at a time around a departure or a homecoming [S2][S3].

Upon return, the employee must be restored to their original position or an equivalent one, keeps benefits accrued before the leave, and cannot be fired or discriminated against for using or asserting these rights [S2][S3].
A worker cannot be forced to substitute accrued vacation or personal days for this leave; substitution is only the worker's choice [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of military family members bear modest costs: they must hold jobs open for up to two weeks of leave, which can be unpaid at their discretion, and they face enforcement rules if they interfere. For most businesses this means temporary coverage gaps rather than direct pay costs.

drawbacks.text: The leave can be unpaid, so a family that most needs the time off may not be able to afford taking it [S2][S3].
Employers, especially small ones, must absorb scheduling disruptions and temporary vacancy when an employee takes leave, and may require certification paperwork before granting it [S2][S3].
The entitlement is narrow: it covers only family members of service members called up or deployed for contingency operations, leaving out other kinds of military service [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but bounded: two weeks of job security around a life-disrupting deployment matters to the roughly military families who need it, and the cost to employers is modest because the leave can be unpaid and requires only a copy of a deployment order as proof. The design is careful rather than sweeping, which makes the bill's failure to get any committee action harder to justify on merits alone.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee, then to its Economic Opportunity Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 21, 2013 by Rep. Matt Cartwright with an initial group of cosponsors [S3].
Referred to the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
On April 2, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, where it remained for the rest of the 113th Congress [S5].
It gathered 40 cosponsors, 38 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but the committee never reported it out and the House never voted on it [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are spared even the modest two-week leave requirement, and members of Congress who opposed or ignored it face no vote on the record. Military families get no new protections.

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Military Family Leave Act of 2013 in the House.

for.name: 40 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, 38 Democrats and 2 Republicans including Rep. Walter Jones.

against.name: House Committee on Veterans' Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee at the end of the 113th Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 2, 2013 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic (38 of 40 cosponsors) with two Republican exceptions; no record of any member voting against the bill because no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill requires employers to hold jobs open for up to two weeks of leave per deployment and limits their ability to force workers to burn paid vacation for it, though the leave can be unpaid. The cost is modest but the industry's preference is to have no leave mandate at all.

industries.industry: Federal contractors and firms employing military families
industries.note: Businesses that employ spouses, children, or parents of deployed service members bear the scheduling and compliance burden, with enforcement provisions allowing workers to sue under existing USERRA-like procedures incorporated from title 38.
